communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: But consider! Count the cost! You know, too, what a black reaction comes upon you. Surely the game is hardly worth the candle. communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: My mind rebels at stagnation. Give me problems, give me work, give me the most abstruse cryptogram or the most intricate analysis, and I am in my own proper atmosphere. I can dispense then with artificial stimulants. But I abhor the dull routine of existence. I crave for mental exaltation. That is why I have chosen my own particular profession,—or rather created it, for I am the only one in the world.

events.label: Holmes identifies himself as the only unofficial consulting detective

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: The only unofficial consulting detective. I am the last and highest court of appeal in detection. When Gregson or Lestrade or Athelney Jones are out of their depths—which, by the way, is their normal state—the matter is laid before me. I examine the data, as an expert, and pronounce a specialist’s opinion. I claim no credit in such cases. My name figures in no newspaper. The work itself, the pleasure of finding a field for my peculiar powers, is my highest reward. But you have yourself had some experience of my methods of work in the Jefferson Hope case.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I glanced over it. Honestly, I cannot congratulate you upon it. Detection is, or ought to be, an exact science, and should be treated in the same cold and unemotional manner. You have attempted to tinge it with romanticism. Some facts should be suppressed, or at least a just sense of proportion should be observed in treating them. The only point in the case which deserved mention was the curious analytical reasoning from effects to causes by which I succeeded in unraveling it.

communicates.content: My practice has extended recently to the Continent. I was consulted last week by François Le Villard, who has come rather to the front lately in the French detective service. He has all the Celtic power of quick intuition, but he is deficient in the wide range of exact knowledge which is essential to the higher developments of his art. The case was concerned with a will, and possessed some features of interest. I was able to refer him to two parallel cases, the one at Riga in 1857, and the other at St. Louis in 1871, which have suggested to him the true solution. Here is the letter which I had this morning acknowledging my assistance.

events.label: Holmes says he has written several technical monographs and describes one on tobacco ashes

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I have been guilty of several monographs. They are all upon technical subjects. Here, for example, is one 'Upon the Distinction between the Ashes of the Various Tobaccoes.' In it I enumerate a hundred and forty forms of cigar-, cigarette-, and pipe-tobacco, with coloured plates illustrating the difference in the ash. It is a point which is continually turning up in criminal trials, and which is sometimes of supreme importance as a clue. If you can say definitely, for example, that some murder has been done by a man who was smoking an Indian lunkah, it obviously narrows your field of search. To the trained eye there is as much difference between the black ash of a Trichinopoly and the white fluff of bird's-eye as there is between a cabbage and a potato.

Just opposite the Wigmore Street Office they have taken up the pavement and thrown up some earth of a peculiar reddish tint. I knew that you had not written a letter, since I sat opposite to you all morning. I see also in your open desk there that you have a sheet of stamps and a thick bundle of post-cards. What could you go into the post-office for, then, but to send a wire? Eliminate all other factors, and the one which remains must be the truth.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I began by stating that your brother was careless. When you observe the lower part of that watch-case you notice that it is not only dinted in two places, but it is cut and marked all over from the habit of keeping other hard objects, such as coins or keys, in the same pocket. Surely it is no great feat to assume that a man who treats a fifty-guinea watch so cavalierly must be a careless man. Neither is it a very far-fetched inference that a man who inherits one article of such value is pretty well provided for in other respects.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes

It is more handy than a label, as there is no risk of the number being lost or transposed. There are no less than four such numbers visible to my lens on the inside of this case. Inference,—that your brother was often at low water. Secondary inference,—that he had occasional bursts of prosperity, or he could not have redeemed the pledge.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Finally, I ask you to look at the inner plate, which contains the key-hole. Look at the thousands of scratches all round the hole,—marks where the key has slipped. What sober man’s key could have scored those grooves? But you will never see a drunkard’s watch without them. He winds it at night, and he leaves these traces of his unsteady hand. Where is the mystery in all this?

What is the use of having powers, doctor, when one has no field upon which to exert them? Crime is commonplace, existence is commonplace, and no qualities save those which are commonplace have any function upon earth.

events.label: Holmes explains the sequence involving Captain Morstan, Major Sholto, and the daughter's gifts

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Captain Morstan disappears. The only person in London whom he could have visited is Major Sholto. Major Sholto denies having heard that he was in London. Four years later Sholto dies. Within a week of his death Captain Morstan’s daughter receives a valuable present, which is repeated from year to year, and now culminates in a letter which describes her as a wronged woman. What wrong can it refer to except this deprivation of her father? And why should the presents begin immediately after Sholto’s death, unless it is that Sholto’s heir knows something of the mystery and desires to make compensation? Have you any alternative theory which will meet the facts?

communicates.content: Bartholomew is a clever fellow. How do you think he found out where the treasure was? He had come to the conclusion that it was somewhere indoors: so he worked out all the cubic space of the house, and made measurements everywhere, so that not one inch should be unaccounted for. Among other things, he found that the height of the building was seventy-four feet, but on adding together the heights of all the separate rooms, and making every allowance for the space between, which he ascertained by borings, he could not bring the total to more than seventy feet. There were four feet unaccounted for. These could only be at the top of the building. He knocked a hole, therefore, in the lath-and-plaster ceiling of the highest room, and there, sure enough, he came upon another little garret above it, which had been sealed up and was known to no one. In the centre stood the treasure-chest, resting upon two rafters. He lowered it through the hole, and there it lies. He computes the value of the jewels at not less than half a million sterling.

communicates.content: Now, Watson, we have half an hour to ourselves. Let us make good use of it. My case is, as I have told you, almost complete; but we must not err on the side of over-confidence. events.label: Holmes explains how the wooden-legged man and an ally could have used the rope to enter and leave through the window

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Quite so. But there has been some one else,—a very able and efficient ally. Could you scale that wall, doctor? Without aid it is so. But suppose you had a friend up here who lowered you this good stout rope which I see in the corner, securing one end of it to this great hook in the wall. Then, I think, if you were an active man, You might swarm up, wooden leg and all. You would depart, of course, in the same fashion, and your ally would draw up the rope, untie it from the hook, shut the window, snib it on the inside, and get away in the way that he originally came. As a minor point it may be noted that our wooden-legged friend, though a fair climber, was not a professional sailor. His hands were far from horny. My lens discloses more than one blood-mark, especially towards the end of the rope, from which I gather that he slipped down with such velocity that he took the skin off his hand.

communicates.content: Do not imagine that I depend for my success in this case upon the mere chance of one of these fellows having put his foot in the chemical. I have knowledge now which would enable me to trace them in many different ways. This, however, is the readiest and, since fortune has put it into our hands, I should be culpable if I neglected it. It has, however, prevented the case from becoming the pretty little intellectual problem which it at one time promised to be. There might have been some credit to be gained out of it, but for this too palpable clue.

events.label: Watson praises Holmes's results and asks how he described the wooden-legged man

communicates.speaker: watson

The thing seems to me to be deeper and more inexplicable. How, for example, could you describe with such confidence the wooden-legged man?

events.label: Holmes explains his deduction about the treasure and the sign of the four

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: it was simplicity itself. I don’t wish to be theatrical. It is all patent and above-board. Two officers who are in command of a convict-guard learn an important secret as to buried treasure. A map is drawn for them by an Englishman named Jonathan Small. You remember that we saw the name upon the chart in Captain Morstan’s possession. He had signed it in behalf of himself and his associates,—the sign of the four, as he somewhat dramatically called it. Aided by this chart, the officers—or one of them—gets the treasure and brings it to England, leaving, we will suppose, some condition under which he received it unfulfilled. Now, then, why did not Jonathan Small get the treasure himself? The answer is obvious. The chart is dated at a time when Morstan was brought into close association with convicts. Jonathan Small did not get the treasure because he and his associates were themselves convicts and could not get away.

Diminutive footmarks, toes never fettered by boots, naked feet, stone-headed wooden mace, great agility, small poisoned darts. What do you make of all this?

events.label: Holmes explains why the footmarks and darts indicate an Andaman islander

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: When first I saw signs of strange weapons I was inclined to think so; but the remarkable character of the footmarks caused me to reconsider my views. Some of the inhabitants of the Indian Peninsula are small men, but none could have left such marks as that. The Hindoo proper has long and thin feet. The sandal-wearing Mohammedan has the great toe well separated from the others, because the thong is commonly passed between. These little darts, too, could only be shot in one way. They are from a blow-pipe. Now, then, where are we to find our savage?

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: South American.

events.label: Holmes consults a gazetteer and reads about the Andaman Islands

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: This is the first volume of a gazetteer which is now being published. It may be looked upon as the very latest authority. Andaman Islands, situated 340 miles to the north of Sumatra, in the Bay of Bengal. Moist climate, coral reefs, sharks, Port Blair, convict-barracks, Rutland Island, cottonwoods. The aborigines of the Andaman Islands may perhaps claim the distinction of being the smallest race upon this earth, though some anthropologists prefer the Bushmen of Africa, the Digger Indians of America, and the Terra del Fuegians. The average height is rather below four feet, although many full-grown adults may be found who are very much smaller than this. They are a fierce, morose, and intractable people, though capable of forming most devoted friendships when their confidence has once been gained. They are naturally hideous, having large, misshapen heads, small, fierce eyes, and distorted features. Their feet and hands, however, are remarkably small. So intractable and fierce are they that all the efforts of the British official have failed to win them over in any degree. They have always been a terror to shipwrecked crews, braining the survivors with their stone-headed clubs, or shooting them with their poisoned arrows. These massacres are invariably concluded by a cannibal feast. Nice, amiable people, Watson! If this fellow had been left to his own unaided devices this affair might have taken an even more ghastly turn. I fancy that, even as it is, Jonathan Small would give a good deal not to have employed him.

events.label: Watson asks how the companion came to be with Small

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: But how came he to have so singular a companion?

events.label: Holmes says he cannot explain how the islander came to be with Small and that they will learn more later

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Ah, that is more than I can tell. Since, however, we had already determined that Small had come from the Andamans, it is not so very wonderful that this islander should be with him. No doubt we shall know all about it in time.

events.label: Holmes tells Watson to lie down on the sofa and tries to put him to sleep with violin music
Watson wakes late in the afternoon, feeling strengthened and refreshed
Holmes sits reading after setting aside his violin
Holmes looks at Watson and his face appears dark and troubled
Holmes says he feared their talk would wake Watson

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You have slept soundly. I feared that our talk would wake you.

events.label: Watson says he heard nothing

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I heard nothing.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Watson has had fresh news

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Have you had fresh news, then?

events.label: Holmes says there is no fresh news and that Wiggins has reported no trace of the launch

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Unfortunately, no. I confess that I am surprised and disappointed. I expected something definite by this time. Wiggins has just been up to report. He says that no trace can be found of the launch. It is a provoking check, for every hour is of importance.

events.label: Watson offers to help and proposes another night outing

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Can I do anything? I am perfectly fresh now, and quite ready for another night’s outing.

events.label: Holmes says they can only wait and that he must remain on guard

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: No, we can do nothing. We can only wait. If we go ourselves, the message might come in our absence, and delay be caused. You can do what you will, but I must remain on guard.

events.label: Watson says he will visit Mrs. Cecil Forrester and Miss Morstan

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Then I shall run over to Camberwell and call upon Mrs. Cecil Forrester. She asked me to, yesterday. Well, of course Miss Morstan too. They were anxious to hear what happened.

events.label: Holmes warns Watson not to tell them too much

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I would not tell them too much. Women are never to be entirely trusted,—not the best of them.

events.label: Watson says he will be back in an hour or two

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I shall be back in an hour or two.

events.label: Holmes wishes Watson luck and asks him to return Toby

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: All right! Good luck! But, I say, if you are crossing the river you may as well return Toby, for I don’t think it is at all likely that we shall have any use for him now.

events.label: Watson takes Toby and leaves him with a half-sovereign at the old naturalist’s in Pinchin Lane
Watson arrives at Camberwell and finds Miss Morstan and Mrs. Forrester waiting to hear the news
Watson tells Miss Morstan and Mrs. Forrester what he and Holmes had done, omitting the worst details

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I told them all that we had done, suppressing, however, the more dreadful parts of the tragedy. Thus, although I spoke of Mr. Sholto’s death, I said nothing of the exact manner and method of it.

events.label: Mrs. Forrester calls the affair a romance

communicates.speaker: mrs_cecil_forrester
communicates.content: It is a romance!

events.label: Mrs. Forrester describes the story with an injured lady, treasure, a black cannibal, and a wooden-legged ruffian

communicates.speaker: mrs_cecil_forrester
communicates.content: An injured lady, half a million in treasure, a black cannibal, and a wooden-legged ruffian. They take the place of the conventional dragon or wicked earl.

events.label: Miss Morstan says two knight-errants are involved in the rescue

communicates.speaker: mary_morstan
communicates.content: And two knight-errants to the rescue.

events.label: Mrs. Forrester says Mary’s fortune depends on the search and comments on riches

communicates.speaker: mrs_cecil_forrester
communicates.content: Why, Mary, your fortune depends upon the issue of this search. I don’t think that you are nearly excited enough. Just imagine what it must be to be so rich, and to have the world at your feet!

events.label: Watson notes Mary shows no elation at the prospect
Miss Morstan says she is anxious for Mr. Thaddeus Sholto and wants him cleared of the charge

communicates.speaker: mary_morstan
communicates.content: It is for Mr. Thaddeus Sholto that I am anxious. Nothing else is of any consequence; but I think that he has behaved most kindly and honourably throughout. It is our duty to clear him of this dreadful and unfounded charge.

events.label: Watson leaves Camberwell and returns home in the dark
Watson finds Holmes absent from home and sees his book and pipe left by the chair
Mrs. Hudson reports that Holmes has gone to his room and worries about his health

communicates.speaker: mrs_hudson
communicates.content: No, sir. He has gone to his room, sir. Do you know, sir, I am afraid for his health?

events.label: Mrs. Hudson describes Holmes walking restlessly and muttering to himself

communicates.speaker: mrs_hudson
communicates.content: Well, he’s that strange, sir. After you was gone he walked and he walked, up and down, and up and down. Then I heard him talking to himself and muttering. And now he has slammed off to his room, but I can hear him walking away the same as ever.

events.label: Mrs. Hudson says she suggested cooling medicine and Holmes reacted sharply

communicates.speaker: mrs_hudson
communicates.content: I ventured to say something to him about cooling medicine, but he turned on me, sir, with such a look that I don’t know how ever I got out of the room.

events.label: Watson reassures Mrs. Hudson about Holmes's condition

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I don’t think that you have any cause to be uneasy, Mrs. Hudson. I have seen him like this before. He has some small matter upon his mind which makes him restless.

events.label: Watson hears Holmes walking through the night and remains uneasy
Holmes appears at breakfast worn and haggard
Watson remarks that Holmes is knocking himself up and had been marching in the night

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: You are knocking yourself up, old man. I heard you marching about in the night.

events.label: Holmes says he could not sleep and explains that the problem is consuming him

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: No, I could not sleep. This infernal problem is consuming me. It is too much to be balked by so petty an obstacle, when all else had been overcome. I know the men, the launch, everything; and yet I can get no news. I have set other agencies at work, and used every means at my disposal. The whole river has been searched on either side, but there is no news, nor has Mrs. Smith heard of her husband. I shall come to the conclusion soon that they have scuttled the craft. But there are objections to that. No, I think that may be dismissed. I had inquiries made, and there is a launch of that description. I have considered that possibility too, and there is a search-party who will work up as far as Richmond. If no news comes to-day, I shall start off myself to-morrow, and go for the men rather than the boat. But surely, surely, we shall hear something.

events.label: No news arrives from Wiggins or the other agencies
Newspaper articles report on the Norwood tragedy and an inquest is scheduled
Watson reports the ill success to the ladies and returns to find Holmes dejected and morose
Holmes works all evening on an abstruse chemical analysis
Watson wakes and finds Holmes standing by his bedside in sailor dress
Holmes says he is going down the river

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I am off down the river, Watson. I have been turning it over in my mind, and I can see only one way out of it. It is worth trying, at all events.

events.label: Watson asks to come with Holmes

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Surely I can come with you, then?

events.label: Holmes instructs Watson to remain as his representative and handle notes and telegrams

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: No; you can be much more useful if you will remain here as my representative. I am loath to go, for it is quite on the cards that some message may come during the day, though Wiggins was despondent about it last night. I want you to open all notes and telegrams, and to act on your own judgment if any news should come. Can I rely upon you? Most certainly. I am afraid that you will not be able to wire to me, for I can hardly tell yet where I may find myself. If I am in luck, however, I may not be gone so very long. I shall have news of some sort or other before I get back.

events.label: Watson has not heard from Holmes by breakfast-time
Watson opens The Standard and finds a fresh allusion to the Upper Norwood tragedy
Watson tosses the paper onto the table and notices an advertisement in the agony column
Watson identifies the advertisement as Holmes's doing
Watson waits through a long day for Holmes or a reply to the advertisement
Watson reflects on Holmes's reasoning and the possibility of error
Athelney Jones arrives to speak with Watson
Watson invites Athelney Jones to wait and offers him a chair, cigars, and whiskey-and-soda
Athelney Jones explains that he has reconsidered his theory about the Norwood case

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: I have been obliged to reconsider it. I had my net drawn tightly round Mr. Sholto, sir, when pop he went through a hole in the middle of it. He was able to prove an alibi which could not be shaken. From the time that he left his brother’s room he was never out of sight of some one or other. So it could not be he who climbed over roofs and through trap-doors. It’s a very dark case, and my professional credit is at stake. I should be very glad of a little assistance.

events.label: Athelney Jones praises Sherlock Holmes and describes receiving a wire from him

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: Your friend Mr. Sherlock Holmes is a wonderful man, sir. He’s a man who is not to be beat. I have known that young man go into a good many cases, but I never saw the case yet that he could not throw a light upon. He is irregular in his methods, and a little quick perhaps in jumping at theories, but, on the whole, I think he would have made a most promising officer, and I don’t care who knows it. I have had a wire from him this morning, by which I understand that he has got some clue to this Sholto business. Here is the message.

events.label: Jones hands Watson a telegram from Holmes

communicates.speaker: telegram
communicates.content: Go to Baker Street at once. If I have not returned, wait for me. I am close on the track of the Sholto gang. You can come with us to-night if you want to be in at the finish.

events.label: Watson comments that Holmes has picked up the scent again

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: This sounds well. He has evidently picked up the scent again.

events.label: Jones responds that Holmes has been at fault too and may be issuing a false alarm

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: Ah, then he has been at fault too. Even the best of us are thrown off sometimes. Of course this may prove to be a false alarm; but it is my duty as an officer of the law to allow no chance to slip.

events.label: An elderly seafaring man arrives at Watson's door and enters
Watson asks the visitor what is the matter

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: What is it, my man?

events.label: The visitor asks whether Sherlock Holmes is present

communicates.speaker: our_visitor
communicates.content: Is Mr. Sherlock Holmes here?

events.label: Watson says he is acting for Holmes and can receive the message

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: No; but I am acting for him. You can tell me any message you have for him.

events.label: The visitor says he was meant to tell Holmes himself

communicates.speaker: our_visitor
communicates.content: It was to him himself I was to tell it.

events.label: Watson insists he is acting for Holmes and asks about Mordecai Smith's boat

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I am acting for him. Was it about Mordecai Smith’s boat?

events.label: The visitor says yes and claims to know the boat, the men, and the treasure

communicates.speaker: our_visitor
communicates.content: Yes. I knows well where it is. An’ I knows where the men he is after are. An’ I knows where the treasure is. I knows all about it.

events.label: Watson asks the visitor to tell him and promises to inform Holmes

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Then tell me, and I shall let him know.

events.label: The visitor repeats that he was to tell Holmes himself

communicates.speaker: our_visitor
communicates.content: It was to him I was to tell it.

events.label: Watson tells the visitor to wait for Holmes

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Well, you must wait for him.

events.label: The visitor refuses to wait and says he will not tell them

communicates.speaker: our_visitor
communicates.content: No, no; I ain’t goin’ to lose a whole day to please no one. If Mr. Holmes ain’t here, then Mr. Holmes must find it all out for himself. I don’t care about the look of either of you, and I won’t tell a word.

events.label: The visitor moves toward the door and Jones blocks him

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: Wait a bit, my friend. You have important information, and you must not walk off. We shall keep you, whether you like or not, until our friend returns.

events.label: The visitor protests that he has been seized and treated badly

communicates.speaker: our_visitor
communicates.content: Pretty sort o’ treatment this! I come here to see a gentleman, and you two, who I never saw in my life, seize me and treat me in this fashion!

events.label: Watson says the visitor will be recompensed and should sit on the sofa

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: You will be none the worse. We shall recompense you for the loss of your time. Sit over here on the sofa, and you will not have long to wait.

events.label: The visitor sits on the sofa
Holmes speaks from close by and asks for a cigar

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I think that you might offer me a cigar too.

events.label: Watson exclaims at seeing Holmes and asks where the old man is

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Holmes! You here! But where is the old man?

events.label: Holmes reveals the old man's disguise

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Here is the old man. Here he is,—wig, whiskers, eyebrows, and all. I thought my disguise was pretty good, but I hardly expected that it would stand that test.

events.label: Jones praises Holmes's disguise and says Holmes did not get away easily

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: Ah, You rogue! You would have made an actor, and a rare one. You had the proper workhouse cough, and those weak legs of yours are worth ten pounds a week. I thought I knew the glint of your eye, though. You didn’t get away from us so easily, You see.

events.label: Holmes says he has worked in disguise all day and asks about the wire

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I have been working in that get-up all day. You see, a good many of the criminal classes begin to know me,—especially since our friend here took to publishing some of my cases: so I can only go on the war-path under some simple disguise like this. You got my wire?

events.label: Jones says the wire brought him there and reports his case has failed

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: Yes; that was what brought me here. It has all come to nothing. I have had to release two of my prisoners, and there is no evidence against the other two.

events.label: Holmes says he will supply two others and puts Jones under his orders

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Never mind. We shall give you two others in the place of them. But you must put yourself under my orders. You are welcome to all the official credit, but you must act on the line that I point out. Is that agreed?

events.label: A plan for a police-boat is arranged at Westminster Stairs for seven o'clock

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: I shall want a fast police-boat—a steam launch—to be at the Westminster Stairs at seven o’clock.

events.label: Jones arranges for two stanch men to be available in the boat

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: I shall want two stanch men, in case of resistance.

events.label: The treasure is to be obtained after the men are secured

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: When we secure the men we shall get the treasure.

events.label: Jones proposes that Watson take the treasure box to the young lady

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: I think that it would be a pleasure to my friend here to take the box round to the young lady to whom half of it rightfully belongs.

events.label: Jones says the treasure must be handed over to the authorities after the official investigation

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: The treasure must afterwards be handed over to the authorities until after the official investigation.

events.label: Holmes requests an unofficial interview with Jonathan Small if he is efficiently guarded

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I should much like to have a few details about this matter from the lips of Jonathan Small himself. There is no objection to my having an unofficial interview with him, either here in my rooms or elsewhere, as long as he is efficiently guarded?

events.label: Jones agrees to the interview if Jonathan Small is caught

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: However, if you can catch him I don’t see how I can refuse you an interview with him.

events.label: Jones insists that Holmes and Watson dine with him

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: Only that I insist upon your dining with us. It will be ready in half an hour.

events.label: Jones remarks that Watson has not yet recognised his merits as a housekeeper

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: Watson, you have never yet recognised my merits as a housekeeper.

events.label: Holmes and the others eat a merry dinner
Holmes pours port and proposes a toast to the success of the expedition

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: One bumper to the success of our little expedition.

events.label: Holmes tells Watson to take a pistol and prepare to leave

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Have you a pistol, Watson? You had best take it, then. It is well to be prepared. I see that the cab is at the door. I ordered it for half-past six.

events.label: Holmes, Watson, and Jones travel by cab to Westminster wharf and board the launch
Jones asks where to go and Holmes directs the launch to the Tower and Jacobson's Yard

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: To the Tower. Tell them to stop opposite Jacobson’s Yard.

events.label: The launch speeds past barges and overtakes a river steamer
Holmes explains how he reconsidered the Sholto problem after chemical analysis and reasoned about Small's likely movements

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I gave my mind a thorough rest by plunging into a chemical analysis. When I had succeeded in dissolving the hydrocarbon which I was at work at, I came back to our problem of the Sholtos, and thought the whole matter out again. ... I then reflected that since he had certainly been in London some time ... he could hardly leave at a moment’s notice, but would need some little time, if it were only a day, to arrange his affairs. That was the balance of probability, at any rate.

events.label: Watson argues that Jonathan Small arranged his affairs before the expedition
Watson reasons that Small kept his lair until he no longer needed it
Watson reasons that Small feared gossip about his companion and the Norwood tragedy
Small and his companion start from headquarters in darkness and return before daylight
Watson infers that the travellers did not go very far
Small and his party pay Smith, reserve the launch, and hurry to their lodgings with the treasure-box
Watson predicts that Small's party will later travel by night to a ship for passage abroad
Watson considers how Small could hide the launch and keep it available
Watson visits the river yards in disguise and asks after the launch
Watson learns that the Aurora was handed over to Jacobson's two days earlier by a wooden-legged man
Mordecai Smith arrives at the yard and calls for the launch that night

communicates.speaker: mordecai_smith
communicates.content: I want her to-night at eight o’clock; eight o’clock sharp, mind, for I have two gentlemen who won’t be kept waiting.

events.label: Smith pays the men with shillings
Watson follows Smith and then returns to the yard
Watson stations a boy to watch the launch and signal when the departure begins
Jones says he would have posted police in Jacobson's Yard and arrested the men when they came down

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: but if the affair were in my hands I should have had a body of police in Jacobson’s Yard, and arrested them when they came down.

events.label: Holmes says Small would send a scout ahead and delay if suspicious

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: This man Small is a pretty shrewd fellow. He would send a scout on ahead, and if anything made him suspicious lie snug for another week.

events.label: Watson suggests sticking to Mordecai Smith to be led to the hiding-place

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: But you might have stuck to Mordecai Smith, and so been led to their hiding-place.

events.label: The boat passes the bridges on the Thames while the conversation continues
The boat passes the City and reaches twilight near the Tower
Holmes identifies Jacobson's Yard and orders the boat to cruise under cover of lighters

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: That is Jacobson’s Yard. Cruise gently up and down here under cover of this string of lighters.

events.label: Holmes looks through night-glasses toward the shore and reports seeing a sentry but no handkerchief

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I see my sentry at his post, but no sign of a handkerchief.

events.label: Jones proposes lying in wait downstream for the men

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: Suppose we go down-stream a short way and lie in wait for them.

events.label: Holmes rejects taking anything for granted and instructs the group to stay put

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: We have no right to take anything for granted. It is certainly ten to one that they go down-stream, but we cannot be certain. From this point we can see the entrance of the yard, and they can hardly see us. It will be a clear night and plenty of light. We must stay where we are. See how the folk swarm over yonder in the gaslight.

events.label: Jones says the people are coming from work in the yard

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: They are coming from work in the yard.

events.label: Holmes speaks about the moral uncertainty of people and statistics

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Dirty-looking rascals, but I suppose every one has some little immortal spark concealed about him. You would not think it, to look at them. There is no a priori probability about it. A strange enigma is man! Winwood Reade is good upon the subject. He remarks that, while the individual man is an insoluble puzzle, in the aggregate he becomes a mathematical certainty. You can, for example, never foretell what any one man will do, but you can say with precision what an average number will be up to. Individuals vary, but percentages remain constant. So says the statistician.

events.label: Holmes spots a white handkerchief in the distance

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Surely there is a white flutter over yonder.

events.label: Watson identifies the flutter as Jones's boy

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Yes, it is your boy. I can see him plainly.

events.label: Holmes sees the Aurora racing downstream and orders pursuit

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Full speed ahead, engineer. Make after that launch with the yellow light. By heaven, I shall never forgive myself if she proves to have the heels of us!

events.label: The Aurora slips unseen through the yard entrance and races down the stream
Jones looks at the Aurora and shakes his head
Holmes urges the stokers to keep feeding the engines so they can catch the Aurora

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Heap it on, stokers! Make her do all she can! If we burn the boat we must have them!

events.label: The pursuing boat follows close behind the Aurora on the river

communicates.speaker: athleney_jones
communicates.content: I think we gain a little.

events.label: A tug with three barges blunders between the pursuers and the Aurora, forcing them to avoid a collision
Jones turns the search-light on the Aurora and the crew on board become visible
Jones yells at the men on the Aurora to stop

communicates.speaker: athleney_jones
communicates.content: Stop.

events.label: Holmes orders fire if the man raises his hand

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Fire if he raises his hand.

events.label: The pursuers close to within touch of their quarry by boat
The white man and the dwarf stand in the boat
The dwarf raises a wooden object to his lips
Holmes and Watson fire their pistols
The dwarf is struck, falls sideways into the stream, and the boatman turns the boat toward the southern bank
The launch runs onto a mud-bank and the fugitive jumps ashore
The fugitive struggles uselessly in the mud
Holmes's party hauls the fugitive out and drags him aboard
The Smiths board the launch when commanded
Holmes's party hauls the Aurora off and makes her fast to the stern
A solid iron chest stands on the deck
Holmes's party transfers the iron chest to their cabin
Holmes and Watson steam upstream and search the river for the Islander
Holmes points to the wooden hatchway
Holmes remarks that they were hardly quick enough with their pistols

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: We were hardly quick enough with our pistols.

events.label: A murderous dart is found stuck behind where the men had been standing
Jonathan Small sits in the cabin opposite the iron box
Jonathan Small appears handcuffed and seated with his head sunk on his breast
Holmes speaks to Jonathan Small and says he is sorry it has come to this

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I am sorry that it has come to this.

events.label: Jonathan Small replies that he is sorry too

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: And so am I, sir.

events.label: Jonathan Small denies striking Mr. Sholto and blames Tonga for shooting him

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: I don’t believe that I can swing over the job. I give you my word on the book that I never raised hand against Mr. Sholto. It was that little hell-hound Tonga who shot one of his cursed darts into him. I had no part in it, sir. I was as grieved as if it had been my blood-relation. I welted the little devil with the slack end of the rope for it, but it was done, and I could not undo it again.

events.label: Holmes offers a cigar and flask and questions how Tonga could overpower Mr. Sholto

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Have a cigar; and you had best take a pull out of my flask, for you are very wet. How could you expect so small and weak a man as this black fellow to overpower Mr. Sholto and hold him while you were climbing the rope?

events.label: Jonathan Small says he hoped to find the room clear and knew the house habits

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: You seem to know as much about it as if you were there, sir. The truth is that I hoped to find the room clear. I knew the habits of the house pretty well, and it was the time when Mr. Sholto usually went down to his supper. I shall make no secret of the business. The best defence that I can make is just the simple truth. Now, if it had been the old major I would have swung for him with a light heart. I would have thought no more of knifing him than of smoking this cigar. But it’s cursed hard that I should be lagged over this young Sholto, with whom I had no quarrel whatever.

events.label: Holmes states that Jonathan Small is under the charge of Athelney Jones and will be brought to his rooms

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You are under the charge of Mr. Athelney Jones, of Scotland Yard. He is going to bring you up to my rooms, and I shall ask you for a true account of the matter. You must make a clean breast of it, for if you do I hope that I may be of use to you. I think I can prove that the poison acts so quickly that the man was dead before ever you reached the room.

events.label: Jonathan Small agrees that the man was dead before he reached the room and describes seeing him

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: That he was, sir. I never got such a turn in my life as when I saw him grinning at me with his head on his shoulder as I climbed through the window. It fairly shook me, sir. I’d have half killed Tonga for it if he had not scrambled off. That was how he came to leave his club, and some of his darts too, as he tells me, which I dare say helped to put you on our track; though how you kept on it is more than I can tell. I don’t feel no malice against you for it.

events.label: Jonathan Small describes his claim to money and his connection with the Agra treasure

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: It does seem a queer thing that I who have a fair claim to nigh upon half a million of money should spend the first half of my life building a breakwater in the Andamans, and am like to spend the other half digging drains at Dartmoor. It was an evil day for me when first I clapped eyes upon the merchant Achmet and had to do with the Agra treasure, which never brought anything but a curse yet upon the man who owned it. To him it brought murder, to Major Sholto it brought fear and guilt, to me it has meant slavery for life.

events.label: Athelney Jones enters the cabin

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: Quite a family party. I think I shall have a pull at that flask, Holmes. Well, I think we may all congratulate each other. Pity we didn’t take the other alive; but there was no choice. I say, Holmes, you must confess that you cut it rather fine. It was all we could do to overhaul her.

events.label: Holmes replies

events.label: Jones reports Smith’s claims about the Aurora and Small’s denial

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: Neither he did, not a word. I chose his launch because I heard that she was a flier. We told him nothing, but we paid him well, and he was to get something handsome if we reached our vessel, the Esmeralda, at Gravesend, outward bound for the Brazils.

events.label: Jones speaks about spare treatment and condemnation

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: Well, if he has done no wrong we shall see that no wrong comes to him. If we are pretty quick in catching our men, we are not so quick in condemning them.

events.label: Narrator observes Jones adopting a self-important manner

communicates.content: We will be at Vauxhall Bridge presently, and shall land you, Dr. Watson, with the treasure-box. I need hardly tell you that I am taking a very grave responsibility upon myself in doing this. It is most irregular; but of course an agreement is an agreement. I must, however, as a matter of duty, send an inspector with you, since you have so valuable a charge. You will drive, no doubt?

communicates.speaker: mrs_cecil_forrester
communicates.content: What news have you brought me?

events.label: Watson says he has brought better than news and a fortune

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I have brought something better than news. I have brought you something which is worth all the news in the world. I have brought you a fortune.

events.label: Mrs. Cecil Forrester comments on the treasure and its value

communicates.speaker: mrs_cecil_forrester
communicates.content: Is that the treasure, then?

events.label: Watson identifies the box as the great Agra treasure and explains the shares

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Yes, this is the great Agra treasure. Half of it is yours and half is Thaddeus Sholto’s. You will have a couple of hundred thousand each. Think of that! An annuity of ten thousand pounds. There will be few richer young ladies in England. Is it not glorious?

events.label: Mrs. Cecil Forrester says she owes the treasure to Watson

communicates.speaker: mrs_cecil_forrester
communicates.content: If I have it, I owe it to you.

events.label: Watson says Sherlock Holmes found the clue and nearly lost the treasure

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: No, no, not to me, but to my friend Sherlock Holmes. With all the will in the world, I could never have followed up a clue which has taxed even his analytical genius. As it was, we very nearly lost it at the last moment.

communicates.speaker: mrs_cecil_forrester
communicates.content: Pray sit down and tell me all about it, Dr. Watson.

events.label: Watson recounts the search, the discovery of the Aurora, Athelney Jones, the expedition, and the chase

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Holmes’s new method of search, the discovery of the Aurora, the appearance of Athelney Jones, our expedition in the evening, and the wild chase down the Thames.

events.label: Mrs. Cecil Forrester reacts to the account of the dart and recovers after water is brought

communicates.speaker: mrs_cecil_forrester
communicates.content: It was a shock to me to hear that I had placed my friends in such horrible peril.

events.label: Watson asks to show the treasure first

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: There is the treasure. What could be brighter than that? I got leave to bring it with me, thinking that it would interest you to be the first to see it.

events.label: Mrs. Cecil Forrester inspects the box and asks for the key and a poker

communicates.speaker: mrs_cecil_forrester
communicates.content: It would be of the greatest interest to me. What a pretty box! This is Indian work, I suppose? And so heavy! The box alone must be of some value. Where is the key?

events.label: Watson says Small threw the key into the Thames

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Small threw it into the Thames.

communicates.speaker: mary_morstan

communicates.speaker: mary_morstan

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Because you are within my reach again. Because I love you, Mary, as truly as ever a man loved a woman. Because this treasure, these riches, sealed my lips. Now that they are gone I can tell you how I love you. That is why I said, 'Thank God.'

events.label: Mary Morstan responds in agreement and the speaker draws her to his side

communicates.speaker: mary_morstan
communicates.content: Then I say, 'Thank God,' too.

events.label: The inspector rides in a cab and waits until Watson rejoins him
Watson shows the inspector the empty box

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Mr. Thaddeus Sholto is a rich man. He will see that you are rewarded, treasure or no.

events.label: The inspector shakes his head despondently

events.label: Jonathan Small declares that he has hidden the treasure and that no one else shall have it

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: Yes, I have put it away where you shall never lay hand upon it. It is my treasure; and if I can’t have the loot I’ll take darned good care that no one else does. I tell you that no living man has any right to it, unless it is three men who are in the Andaman convict-barracks and myself. I know now that I cannot have the use of it, and I know that they cannot. I have acted all through for them as much as for myself. It’s been the sign of four with us always. Well I know that they would have had me do just what I have done, and throw the treasure into the Thames rather than let it go to kith or kin of Sholto or of Morstan. It was not to make them rich that we did for Achmet. You’ll find the treasure where the key is, and where little Tonga is. When I saw that your launch must catch us, I put the loot away in a safe place. There are no rupees for you this journey.

communicates.content: You are deceiving us, Small. If you had wished to throw the treasure into the Thames it would have been easier for you to have thrown box and all.

events.label: Jonathan Small replies that throwing the box would have made recovery easier

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: Easier for me to throw, and easier for you to recover. The man that was clever enough to hunt me down is clever enough to pick an iron box from the bottom of a river. Now that they are scattered over five miles or so, it may be a harder job. It went to my heart to do it, though. I was half mad when you came up with us. However, there’s no good grieving over it. I’ve had ups in my life, and I’ve had downs, but I’ve learned not to cry over spilled milk.

events.label: The detective says Small would have had a better chance at his trial if he had helped justice

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: This is a very serious matter, Small. If you had helped justice, instead of thwarting it in this way, you would have had a better chance at your trial.

events.label: Jonathan Small denounces justice and claims to have earned the treasure through suffering

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: Justice! A pretty justice! Whose loot is this, if it is not ours? Where is the justice that I should give it up to those who have never earned it? Look how I have earned it! Twenty long years in that fever-ridden swamp, all day at work under the mangrove-tree, all night chained up in the filthy convict-huts, bitten by mosquitoes, racked with ague, bullied by every cursed black-faced policeman who loved to take it out of a white man. That was how I earned the Agra treasure; and you talk to me of justice because I cannot bear to feel that I have paid this price only that another may enjoy it! I would rather swing a score of times, or have one of Tonga’s darts in my hide, than live in a convict’s cell and feel that another man is at his ease in a palace with the money that should be mine.

events.label: Small drops his mask of stoicism and speaks wildly while his handcuffs clank

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You forget that we know nothing of all this. We have not heard your story, and we cannot tell how far justice may originally have been on your side.

events.label: John Small responds that he bears no grudge and will tell his story

communicates.speaker: john_small
communicates.content: Well, sir, you have been very fair-spoken to me, though I can see that I have you to thank that I have these bracelets upon my wrists. Still, I bear no grudge for that. It is all fair and above-board. If you want to hear my story I have no wish to hold it back. What I say to you is God’s truth, every word of it. Thank you; you can put the glass beside me here, and I’ll put my lips to it if I am dry.

events.label: John Small states that he is a Worcestershire man born near Pershore

communicates.speaker: john_small
communicates.content: I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore. I dare say you would find a heap of Smalls living there now if you were to look.

events.label: John Small says he had been no credit to his family and had been a rover

communicates.speaker: john_small
communicates.content: I have often thought of taking a look round there, but the truth is that I was never much of a credit to the family, and I doubt if they would be so very glad to see me. They were all steady, chapel-going folk, small farmers, well-known and respected over the country-side, while I was always a bit of a rover.

events.label: John Small joins the 3rd Buffs and goes to India

communicates.speaker: john_small
communicates.content: At last, however, when I was about eighteen, I gave them no more trouble, for I got into a mess over a girl, and could only get out of it again by taking the Queen’s shilling and joining the 3rd Buffs, which was just starting for India.

events.label: John Small swims in the Ganges and is attacked by a crocodile

communicates.speaker: john_small
communicates.content: I wasn’t destined to do much soldiering, however. I had just got past the goose-step, and learned to handle my musket, when I was fool enough to go swimming in the Ganges. Luckily for me, my company sergeant, John Holder, was in the water at the same time, and he was one of the finest swimmers in the service. A crocodile took me, just as I was half-way across, and nipped off my right leg as clean as a surgeon could have done it, just above the knee. What with the shock and the loss of blood, I fainted, and should have drowned if Holder had not caught hold of me and paddled for the bank. I was five months in hospital over it, and when at last I was able to limp out of it with this timber toe strapped to my stump I found myself invalided out of the army and unfitted for any active occupation.

events.label: John Small says he became a cripple and was left unable to work actively

communicates.speaker: john_small
communicates.content: I was, as you can imagine, pretty down on my luck at this time, for I was a useless cripple though not yet in my twentieth year. However, my misfortune soon proved to be a blessing in disguise.

events.label: Abel White offers John Small an overseer post and the colonel recommends him

communicates.speaker: john_small
communicates.content: A man named Abel White, who had come out there as an indigo-planter, wanted an overseer to look after his coolies and keep them up to their work. He happened to be a friend of our colonel’s, who had taken an interest in me since the accident. To make a long story short, the colonel recommended me strongly for the post and, as the work was mostly to be done on horseback, my leg was no great obstacle, for I had enough knee left to keep good grip on the saddle. What I had to do was to ride over the plantation, to keep an eye on the men as they worked, and to report the idlers. The pay was fair, I had comfortable quarters, and altogether I was content to spend the remainder of my life in indigo-planting. Mr. Abel White was a kind man, and he would often drop into my little shanty and smoke a pipe with me, for white folk out there feel their hearts warm to each other as they never do here at home.

The thing stands thus, Sahib, and I tell it to you because I know that an oath is binding upon a Feringhee, and that we may trust you. Had you been a lying Hindoo, though you had sworn by all the gods in their false temples, your blood would have been upon the knife, and your body in the water. But the Sikh knows the Englishman, and the Englishman knows the Sikh. Hearken, then, to what I have to say.

events.label: Mahomet Singh describes a rajah's wealth, concealment, and alliance choices

communicates.speaker: mahomet_singh
communicates.content: There is a rajah in the northern provinces who has much wealth, though his lands are small. Much has come to him from his father, and more still he has set by himself, for he is of a low nature and hoards his gold rather than spend it. When the troubles broke out he would be friends both with the lion and the tiger,—with the Sepoy and with the Company’s Raj. Soon, however, it seemed to him that the white men’s day was come, for through all the land he could hear of nothing but of their death and their overthrow. Yet, being a careful man, he made such plans that, come what might, half at least of his treasure should be left to him. That which was in gold and silver he kept by him in the vaults of his palace, but the most precious stones and the choicest pearls that he had he put in an iron box, and sent it by a trusty servant who, under the guise of a merchant, should take it to the fort at Agra, there to lie until the land is at peace. Thus, if the rebels won he would have his money, but if the Company conquered his jewels would be saved to him. Having thus divided his hoard, he threw himself into the cause of the Sepoys, since they were strong upon his borders. By doing this, mark you, Sahib, his property becomes the due of those who have been true to their salt.

He has with him as travelling-companion my foster-brother Dost Akbar, who knows his secret. Dost Akbar has promised this night to lead him to a side-postern of the fort, and has chosen this one for his purpose. Here he will come presently, and here he will find Mahomet Singh and myself awaiting him. The place is lonely, and none shall know of his coming. The world shall know of the merchant Achmet no more, but the great treasure of the rajah shall be divided among us. What say you to it, Sahib?

communicates.content: This is a very important matter, Small. You must not say a word to any one about it, and I shall see you again soon.

events.label: The major and Captain Morstan come to Small's hut at night with a lantern
The major asks Small to let Captain Morstan hear the story

communicates.speaker: major
communicates.content: I want you just to let Captain Morstan hear that story from your own lips, Small.

events.label: Small repeats the story

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: the story

events.label: The major asks whether the story rings true and is good enough to act upon

communicates.speaker: major
communicates.content: It rings true, eh? It's good enough to act upon?

events.label: Captain Morstan nods
The major explains that the secret is a private concern and asks what price Small would ask for it

communicates.speaker: major
communicates.content: We have been talking it over, my friend here and I, and we have come to the conclusion that this secret of yours is hardly a government matter, after all, but is a private concern of your own, which of course you have the power of disposing of as you think best. Now, the question is, what price would you ask for it? We might be inclined to take it up, and at least look into it, if we could agree as to terms.

events.label: Small proposes a bargain for his freedom and the freedom of his three companions

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: there is only one bargain which a man in my position can make. I shall want you to help me to my freedom, and to help my three companions to theirs. We shall then take you into partnership, and give you a fifth share to divide between you.

events.label: The major objects that a fifth share is not very tempting

communicates.speaker: major
communicates.content: A fifth share! That is not very tempting.

events.label: Small says the share would come to fifty thousand apiece

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: It would come to fifty thousand apiece.

events.label: The major says gaining Small's freedom is impossible

communicates.speaker: major
communicates.content: But how can we gain your freedom? You know very well that you ask an impossibility.

events.label: Small explains the plan to escape by boat with provisions

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: Nothing of the sort. I have thought it all out to the last detail. The only bar to our escape is that we can get no boat fit for the voyage, and no provisions to last us for so long a time. There are plenty of little yachts and yawls at Calcutta or Madras which would serve our turn well. Do you bring one over. We shall engage to get aboard her by night, and if you will drop us on any part of the Indian coast you will have done your part of the bargain.

events.label: The major says he could agree only if there were one prisoner

communicates.speaker: major
communicates.content: If there were only one.

events.label: Small replies that it must be all or none and that the four must act together

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: None or all. We have sworn it. The four of us must always act together.

events.label: The major tells Morstan that Small is a man of his word and may be trusted

communicates.speaker: major
communicates.content: Small is a man of his word. He does not flinch from his friend. I think we may very well trust him.

events.label: Captain Morstan says the business is dirty but the money would help their commissions

communicates.speaker: captain_morstan
communicates.content: It's a dirty business, yet, as you say, the money would save our commissions handsomely.

events.label: The major agrees to try to meet Small and asks him where the box is hidden

communicates.speaker: major
communicates.content: We must, I suppose, try and meet you. We must first, of course, test the truth of your story. Tell me where the box is hid, and I shall get leave of absence and go back to India in the monthly relief-boat to inquire into the affair.

events.label: The speaker demands the consent of his three comrades before agreeing

communicates.speaker: narrator
communicates.content: I must have the consent of my three comrades. I tell you that it is four or none with us. Black or blue, they are in with me, and we all go together.

events.label: A second meeting is held with the three comrades present
The parties agree on the treasure-plan arrangement

communicates.speaker: narrator
communicates.content: We were to provide both the officers with charts of the part of the Agra fort and mark the place in the wall where the treasure was hid. Major Sholto was to go to India to test our story. If he found the box he was to leave it there, to send out a small yacht provisioned for a voyage, which was to lie off Rutland Island, and to which we were to make our way, and finally to return to his duties. Captain Morstan was then to apply for leave of absence, to meet us at Agra, and there we were to have a final division of the treasure, he taking the major’s share as well as his own. All this we sealed by the most solemn oaths that the mind could think or the lips utter.

events.label: The two charts are prepared and signed
Major Sholto goes to India
Captain Morstan appears on a passenger list in a mail-boat
Major Sholto inherits a fortune and leaves the army
Captain Morstan goes to Agra and finds the treasure gone
The speaker resolves to seek vengeance against Sholto
The speaker takes an Andaman Islander into his care and cures him
The narrator arranges an escape with Tonga

communicates.speaker: narrator
communicates.content: He is to bring his boat round on a certain night to an old wharf which is never guarded, and there he is to pick me up. He is to have several gourds of water and a lot of yams, cocoa-nuts, and sweet potatoes.

events.label: Tonga brings his boat to the wharf
The narrator attacks the convict-guard with his wooden leg and kills him
The narrator reaches Tonga's boat and leaves the shore
Tonga carries his possessions, including arms, gods, a bamboo spear, and matting
The narrator and Tonga are picked up by a trader carrying Malay pilgrims
The narrator and Tonga drift about the world and later reach England
The narrator searches for Sholto in England and discovers that he still has the jewels
The narrator tries various ways to get at Sholto
The narrator receives word that Bartholomew Sholto is dying
The narrator goes to the garden and sees Bartholomew Sholto in bed with his sons beside him
Bartholomew Sholto dies
The narrator enters Bartholomew Sholto's room and searches his papers for a record of the hidden jewels
The narrator leaves the room bitter and savage
The narrator scrawls the sign of the four and pins it on Bartholomew Sholto's bosom
The narrator and Tonga earn a living by exhibiting Tonga at fairs and other places
The narrator hears news from Pondicherry Lodge over the years
The treasure is found in Bartholomew Sholto's chemical laboratory
The narrator goes to inspect the place but cannot reach it with his wooden leg
The narrator learns about the trap-door in the roof and Mr. Sholto's supper-hour
The narrator brings Tonga out with a rope wound round his waist
Tonga climbs through the roof into the room
Tonga kills Bartholomew Sholto
The narrator comes up by the rope and finds Tonga strutting about
The narrator strikes at Tonga with the rope's end and curses him
The narrator takes the treasure-box, lowers it down, and slides down himself after leaving the sign of the four on the table
Tonga pulls up the rope, closes the window, and leaves
The narrator hears about Smith's launch Aurora and decides it is suitable for escape
The narrator engages with Mordecai Smith and offers a large sum if he gets them safe to their ship

communicates.speaker: narrator
communicates.content: I engage with old Smith, and was to give him a big sum if he got us safe to our ship.

events.label: Mordecai Smith remains outside the narrator's secrets
The narrator tells gentlemen that he is telling the truth and explains his defence

communicates.speaker: narrator
communicates.content: All this is the truth, and if I tell it to you, gentlemen, it is not to amuse you,—for you have not done me a very good turn,—but it is because I believe the best defence I can make is just to hold back nothing, but let all the world know how badly I have myself been served by Major Sholto, and how innocent I am of the death of his son.

events.label: Holmes comments that Tonga had lost all his darts except the one in his blow-pipe and that one was shot at them in the boat

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There is nothing at all new to me in the latter part of your narrative, except that you brought your own rope. That I did not know. By the way, I had hoped that Tonga had lost all his darts; yet he managed to shoot one at us in the boat.

events.label: The convict replies that Tonga had lost all the darts except the one in his blow-pipe

communicates.speaker: convict
communicates.content: He had lost them all, sir, except the one which was in his blow-pipe at the time.

events.label: The convict asks whether there is any other point to ask about

communicates.speaker: convict
communicates.content: Is there any other point which you would like to ask about?

events.label: Watson answers that he does not think so and thanks the convict

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I think not, thank you.

events.label: Athelney Jones says he will feel more at ease when the story-teller is safe under lock and key, notes that the cab still waits and two inspectors are downstairs, thanks Holmes and Watson, says they will be wanted at the trial, and bids good-night

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: You are a man to be humoured, and we all know that you are a connoisseur of crime, but duty is duty, and I have gone rather far in doing what you and your friend asked me. I shall feel more at ease when we have our story-teller here safe under lock and key. The cab still waits, and there are two inspectors downstairs. I am much obliged to you both for your assistance. Of course you will be wanted at the trial. Good-night to you.

events.label: Jonathan Small bids the gentlemen good-night

communicates.speaker: jonathan_small
communicates.content: Good-night, gentlemen both.

events.label: Jones warns Jonathan Small to go first and says he will take care that Small does not club him with his wooden leg

communicates.speaker: athelney_jones
communicates.content: You first, Small. I’ll take particular care that you don’t club me with your wooden leg, whatever you may have done to the gentleman at the Andaman Isles.

events.label: Watson remarks that the little drama has ended and that they have sat smoking in silence

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Well, and there is the end of our little drama.

events.label: Watson says he fears it may be the last investigation in which he shall study Holmes's methods

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I fear that it may be the last investigation in which I shall have the chance of studying your methods.

events.label: Watson says Miss Morstan has accepted him as a husband in prospective

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Miss Morstan has done me the honour to accept me as a husband in prospective.

events.label: Holmes groans, says he feared as much, and says he cannot congratulate Watson

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I feared as much. I really cannot congratulate you.

events.label: Watson asks whether Holmes has any reason to be dissatisfied with his choice

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Have you any reason to be dissatisfied with my choice?

events.label: Holmes says he thinks Miss Morstan charming, praises her usefulness, cites her preservation of the Agra plan, explains that love is emotional and opposed to cold reason, and says he would never marry

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Not at all. I think she is one of the most charming young ladies I ever met, and might have been most useful in such work as we have been doing. She had a decided genius that way: witness the way in which she preserved that Agra plan from all the other papers of her father. But love is an emotional thing, and whatever is emotional is opposed to that true cold reason which I place above all things. I should never marry myself, lest I bias my judgment.

events.label: Watson says he trusts his judgment may survive the ordeal and remarks that Holmes looks weary

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I trust that my judgment may survive the ordeal. But you look weary.

events.label: Holmes says the reaction is already upon him and that he will be limp as a rag for a week

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Yes, the reaction is already upon me. I shall be as limp as a rag for a week.

events.label: Watson remarks on Holmes's alternation of laziness with energy and vigour

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Strange, how terms of what in another man I should call laziness alternate with your fits of splendid energy and vigour.

events.label: Holmes says he has the makings of a loafer and a spry fellow and quotes Goethe

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Yes, there are in me the makings of a very fine loafer and also of a pretty spry sort of fellow. I often think of those lines of old Goethe,— Schade dass die Natur nur einen Mensch aus Dir schuf, Denn zum würdigen Mann war und zum Schelmen der Stoff.

events.label: Holmes says Lal Rao was the confederate in the house and that Jones has the undivided honour of having caught one fish in his haul

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: By the way, à propos of this Norwood business, you see that they had, as I surmised, a confederate in the house, who could be none other than Lal Rao, the butler: so Jones actually has the undivided honour of having caught one fish in his great haul.

events.label: Watson says the division seems unfair, Holmes did all the work, Jones gets the credit, and Watson gets a wife

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: The division seems rather unfair. You have done all the work in this business. I get a wife out of it, Jones gets the credit, pray what remains for you?

events.label: Sherlock Holmes says that the cocaine-bottle remains

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: For me, there still remains the cocaine-bottle.
