clues.significance: Holmes inferred that the distinctive tobacco ash could serve as a clue in criminal trials and narrow the search for a murderer.
Holmes inferred that Watson's brother was careless from the dents and scratches on the watch-case.
Holmes inferred that Watson's brother was often at low water and had occasional bursts of prosperity from the pawn-ticket numbers inside the case.
Holmes inferred that Watson's brother was a drunkard from the key-hole scratches on the watch.
Holmes inferred that the letter and the pearl-box addresses were written by the same person from the matching disguised hand and recurring Greek e and final s forms.
Holmes inferred that the paper was a native Indian-made document pinned to a board and showing a building plan with the inscription 'The sign of the four' and the four names.
Holmes used the pocket-book as an item that may prove useful to the investigation.
The elder brother found a torn paper on the father's chest marked with 'The sign of the four', which indicated a secret visitor had rifled the room.
Thaddeus Sholto treated the chaplet as evidence of the missing riches and used it to judge their splendour.
Bartholomew Sholto inferred the treasure's hidden location by calculating the house's cubic space, finding four feet unaccounted for, and discovering a sealed garret with the treasure-chest inside.
Watson observed that the face in the room was the face of Bartholomew Sholto, whom Holmes and Watson were seeking.
Holmes inferred that the note contained an important case marker when he examined the torn paper and handed it to Watson.
Holmes inferred that the death was caused by a poisoned thorn found above the ear.
Holmes inferred that the mud marks on the sill were the impression of a wooden stump, identifying the wooden-legged man as the climber.
Holmes inferred that a rope had been used to climb the wall and that the ally drew it up afterward from the blood marks and its position in the corner.
Holmes inferred that the maker of the footmarks was exceptionally small from the size of the naked footprints
Holmes inferred that the poison had entered the victim through a thorn driven or shot into the scalp.
Holmes inferred that the splinter in the man's scalp was poisoned.
Holmes treated the card as part of the evidence on the table.
Holmes identified the stone-headed instrument as an item lying beside the card.
Athelney Jones inferred that the man got away through the trap-door to the roof.
Holmes inferred that the footmarks belonged to a child or a small woman, and he noted that the right-foot print had toes distinctly divided rather than cramped together.
Holmes inferred that the man had put his foot out through the flap-window edge from the strong tarry smell.
Holmes inferred that the dropped pouch confirmed the route the man had taken and that he had dropped it in his hurry.
Holmes identified the spines in the pouch as dangerous objects associated with the attack on Bartholomew Sholto.
Holmes used the creasote scent as the trail that the dog could follow.
Holmes used the handkerchief to test the dog and then as a scent source for the pursuit.
Holmes inferred that blood was present on the white plaster from the slight smudge he observed.
Holmes inferred that Jonathan Small had entered the room at night and left a record of his visit from the inscribed card.
Holmes inferred the presence of an associate from the creasote on the naked foot and the resulting limping track associated with Toby.
Holmes inferred that Jonathan Small had lowered the treasure-box to the ground before continuing the pursuit.
Holmes inferred that the scent trail ended at the barrel when Toby sprang upon it at the timber-yard.
Holmes identified the dark liquid on the barrel and trolley as creasote by its smell.
Holmes inferred that the trail had been crossed because creasote was widely carted about London and used for seasoning wood.
Holmes found the body of Bartholomew Sholto at Pondicherry Lodge and this led to the murder investigation.
Jones treated the missing Indian gems as stolen property connected to the murder case.
Holmes inferred that the culprit was not an Indian Peninsula inhabitant because the footmarks were too small and matched an Andaman islander more closely.
Holmes used the gazetteer entry on the Andaman Islands to identify the likely origin of the savage and the companion with Jonathan Small.
Watson inferred that Holmes had placed the Baker Street advertisement because the address proved it.
Watson inferred that the launch was concealed at a yard because the Aurora had been handed over to Jacobson's with a trivial rudder direction and Smith later came to claim her there.
Holmes inferred that the expected signal had appeared when he spotted the white handkerchief fluttering over yonder.
Holmes identified the iron chest as the same one that had contained the ill-omened treasure of the Sholtos.
Holmes found that a murderous dart had whizzed between them at the instant they fired.
Holmes used the iron box as the central object that Jonathan Small had waited long to gain and treated it as the cause of the captive's wrongdoing.
Watson found that the box was empty after opening it, so the supposed treasure was not inside.
Watson learned that the bundle contained an iron box holding personal family matters that the merchant said he did not want to lose.
Little merchant identified the Great Mogul as one of the diamonds in the treasure and noted that it was said to be the second largest stone in existence.
No clue inference is explicitly attributed to a specific character in this section; the jewels were linked to the trial and later became unimportant after the rajah's fall.
The narrator revealed that he knew where half a million worth of treasure lay and that the real owner was outlawed, so the treasure belonged to the first comer.
The narrator used the sign of the four as a mark of hatred and as a token showing the jewels had returned to those who had most right to them.
The narrator took the treasure-box after Tonga killed Bartholomew Sholto and recovered the jewels.
Holmes inferred that Tonga had lost all his darts except the one in his blow-pipe and that one was the dart used against them in the boat.
